what_its_for: Velaglucerase alfa is used to treat adults and children (4 years and older) with Type 1 Gaucher disease. Gaucher disease causes a fatty substance to build up in your organs and bones because your body is missing an important enzyme. This medicine replaces that missing enzyme so your body can break down the fatty substance properly. It can help reduce the size of your spleen and liver, improve blood counts, and reduce bone problems.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as an intravenous (IV) infusion, meaning it is slowly dripped into your vein through a needle or catheter. It is given by a healthcare provider in a clinic, hospital, or infusion center. Each infusion takes about 60 minutes. You will be monitored during and after your infusion for any reactions.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your weight. The typical dose is 60 units per kilogram (units/kg) of body weight, given every other week (every 2 weeks). Your doctor may adjust your dose depending on how well your body responds to the treatment. Never change your dose on your own — always follow your doctor's instructions.
missed_dose: If you miss or skip an infusion appointment, contact your doctor or infusion center as soon as possible to reschedule. Try not to miss doses, as staying on a regular schedule is important for this medicine to work well. Do not try to give yourself a double dose to make up for a missed one.
storage: Velaglucerase alfa is stored and prepared by healthcare professionals. The unreconstituted (powder) vials should be kept in the refrigerator between 36°F and 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Keep vials in the original carton to protect them from light. Once the medicine is mixed and diluted, it should be used within 24 hours if kept in the refrigerator. Do not freeze. Keep out of reach of children.
what_to_avoid: There are no specific foods, drinks, or activities you need to strictly avoid while taking this medicine. However, let your healthcare team know before starting if you have had any previous allergic reactions to enzyme replacement therapies. Also tell your doctor about all other medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take to avoid any possible interactions.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to an emergency room right away if you experience any of the following during or after your infusion: difficulty breathing, chest tightness, wheezing, severe dizziness, fainting, rapid heartbeat, swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat, severe rash or hives, or a sudden drop in blood pressure. Also contact your doctor if you notice unusual bruising or bleeding, persistent fatigue, worsening bone pain, fever, or any new or concerning symptoms.
when_it_works: Most patients begin to notice improvements within the first 6 to 12 months of treatment. You may see your spleen and liver get smaller and your blood counts (like hemoglobin and platelet levels) improve. Bone symptoms may take longer to improve — sometimes a year or more. Everyone responds differently, so be patient and keep all your follow-up appointments so your doctor can monitor your progress.
special_populations: Children (ages 4 and older): This medicine is approved and has been studied in children, and the dosing is based on body weight just like in adults. Pregnant or breastfeeding women: Tell your doctor right away if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. There is limited safety data in pregnancy, so your doctor will carefully weigh the benefits and risks. Elderly patients: There is limited information on use in patients 65 years and older, so your doctor will monitor you closely. Patients with prior allergic reactions to other enzyme replacement therapies: Let your doctor know, as you may need extra monitoring or pre-treatment with antihistamines or steroids.
